lesson.title: The Audio Frequency Range: Engineering to Match the Ear
lesson.summary: The audio frequency range is the band of frequencies, roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, that audio electronics are designed to carry faithfully because it matches the human hearing range.
lesson.body:
Human hearing range describes what the ear can perceive. Audio frequency range is the engineering term for the band of frequencies that audio equipment, amplifiers, microphones, speakers, and filters are designed to pass through with minimal distortion, and it is deliberately set to match the human hearing range of approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz. When a specification sheet for an amplifier says its frequency response is 20 Hz to 20 kHz, it means the circuit was designed so that frequencies inside that window are reproduced at close to their original level, while frequencies outside it are allowed to roll off, because reproducing them faithfully would not improve what a listener actually hears.

Audio engineers commonly split the audio frequency range into rough sub bands to describe where different filters and controls act: bass roughly 20 Hz to 250 Hz, midrange roughly 250 Hz to 4,000 Hz, and treble roughly 4,000 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Checking the octave math confirms these sub bands tile the whole range consistently: bass spans log2(250/20) = log2(12.5) = 3.64 octaves, midrange spans log2(4000/250) = log2(16) = 4 octaves exactly, and treble spans log2(20000/4000) = log2(5) = 2.32 octaves. Adding 3.64 + 4 + 2.32 gives 9.96 octaves, matching, within normal rounding, the roughly 9.97 octave span of the full audio frequency range from the previous section, since 20 times 12.5 times 16 times 5 is exactly 20,000, the same ratio calculated directly.

These sub band boundaries are not laws of physics, they are practical engineering conventions, and different manufacturers draw the lines in slightly different places. What matters for the rest of this chapter is the idea itself: a bass filter is a circuit tuned to act mainly in that roughly 20 to 250 Hz region, a treble filter acts mainly in the roughly 4 kHz to 20 kHz region, and both are built on top of the audio frequency range concept introduced here.
